title: Learning Locally, Revising Globally: Global Reviser for Federated Learning with Noisy Labels
claim: Under noisy labels, the federated global model memorizes far fewer noisy labels and avoids the test-accuracy decline that centralized training shows.
layout: 2x2 grid of line plots; rows are memorization and test accuracy, columns are IID and non-IID
description: A 2x2 grid of line plots on a light gray background with white gridlines. The top row, labeled (a), plots memorization percentage against centralized epochs or FL rounds, 0 to 200, for IID data on the left and Non-IID Dirichlet-0.3 data on the right. A blue centralized curve climbs steeply toward a red dashed line marking the overall noise ratio. An orange curve (FL, local epoch 1) stays near zero. A green curve (FL, local epoch 10) fluctuates around 5%. The bottom row, labeled (b), plots test accuracy over the same axes. The blue centralized curve peaks early and then drops, while the orange and green FL curves keep rising or stay stable. Each plot has a legend inside it. The eye goes first to the blue curve's divergence from the orange and green curves.
caption: (a) Slower Memorization Effect: On CIFAR-10, the global FL model memorizes $\leq$30% of noisy labels, while significantly lower than that of centralized training. (b) Preservation of Test Performance: The global model in FL avoids the test performance degradation typically observed in centralized training under noisy labels. Please see appendix [ref] for more results and discussions, which indicates that such a phenomenon is non-trivial.
abstract: Conventional federated learning (FL) heavily depends on high-quality labels, which are often impractical in the real world, leading to the federated label-noise (F-LN) problem. Worse still, the F-LN problem is exacerbated by the heterogeneity of FL, whereas clients experience different label-noise types, ratios, and data distribution. In this study, we first observe an intriguing phenomenon that the global model of FL exhibits a slow memorization of noisy labels, suggesting its ability to maintain reliable predictions and robust representations in FL. Motivated by this, we propose a novel method termed Federated Global Reviser (\method), a straightforward yet effective method comprising three modules that collaboratively rectify noisy labels and regularize local training. By exploiting this inherent property, \method\ improves the label-noise robustness of FL in a self-contained manner. Extensive experiments on three widely used F-LN benchmarks demonstrate the superior performance of FedGR, consistently outperforming eight state-of-the-art baselines even in severe label-noise and data heterogeneity.
